speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-84
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have had to make a speech several times on government time allocation motions, so it is getting to be a bit of a habit.
I am sorry that the hon. member for Prince Albert finds the speeches boring. If he paid closer attention, he probably would be able to glean germs of truth about the autocratic and dictatorial way that this government treats the House of Commons. He is going to get another 10-minute lecture on it this morning, I am afraid to say. I have some facts and figures that I think will amuse hon. members opposite when they consider how dictatorial their efforts have been.

Government Orders
I want to turn particularly to the record of this House during this session of Parliament which has gone on for almost two years, it started in April 1989, so that members can hear the litany of time allocation and closure that has been used throughout the session of Parliament. First of all, I want to look at the raw data. The fact is that in the official statistics produced by the Table, it is evident that 294 hours and 41 minutes have been spent considering second reading of government bills. I will repeat that figure for the hon. member for Cariboo-Chilcotin. He looks interested: 294 hours and 41 minutes.
There have been 82 government bills that have received second reading, from my quick count of the records. This means that the average time spent on second reading debate through this session has been 2.14 hours per government bill. That is not excessive, and yet here we have time allocation once again.
On third readings, the total time spent is 94 hours and 27 minutes. Some 53 government bills have already received third reading, and they say we are holding things up. Imagine, 53 government bills which have received third reading. That means 1.7 hours of debate per bill at third reading, and this is considered excessive by hon. members opposite. I find their approach to Parliament absolutely incredible. Their attempts are always to ram things through.
Let us look at the record. I keep citing these figures; they seem to fall on deaf ears. Closure has been used in this Parliament, that is since November 1988, a total of 13 times by this government. Then there is time allocation-and I am separating the two for the purpose of this discussion-which has been used seven times until today. This is number eight. That is seven times previously and eight times so far in this Parliament.
But that is only part of the story. If we look back at the lamentable record of government members since May 1985 when they started using time allocation, they have now used it on a cumulative basis 25 times in five years, from 1985 to 1990. They have threatened to use it on at least four other occasions when they proposed time allocation and then either withdrew it or had it thrown
out by the Speaker, as they did in October of this year, because the Minister of State for Privatization, who got up and once again made an error as he did this morning in not making a speech first, tried to propose time allocation at second reading of this bill. We in the opposition, ever vigilant of Parliament's rights, got up and urged the Speaker to chuck that notice out, and he did. Therefore the minister was unable to move it as quickly as he would have liked.
If we count the attempts-and I see the minister has reappeared-we will find it has been 31 times that the government has either attempted or succeeded in using time allocation in debates in a five-year period. In the 19 previous years, Liberal governments used it a total of 29 times. On any comparison this government has gone hog wild in trampling on the rights of Parliament to debate.
I would like to quote some words. I found some quotations as I was browsing through books last evening. Perhaps hon. members opposite would care to guess whose words these are. I will first quote this line:
Professor Ivor Jennings, the great English authority on Parliament said-and rightly-that "the function of Parliament is not to govern but to criticize, to modify Government policy, and to educate public opinion", lb those who say that Parliament should be turning out legislation in quantity, my answer is that its mission is freedom and the assurance that all the people shall receive justice. It is not a slot machine into which one drops a slug to see the legislation come out.
Who said those words? Was it a great Liberal Prime Minister of Canada? No. Was it one of the members of the present government? No, certainly not. One would not expect to hear those words from the present government, the way it tramples on Parliament's rights. I will tell the House who it was. It was a previous leader of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada and a former Prime Minister of this country, the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker. He said these words. Let's hear them again. When referring to Parliament he said:
-its mission is freedom and the assurance that all the people shall receive justice. It is not a slot machine into which one drops a slug to see the legislation come out.
Yet this government and in particular the government House leader take the view that if Parliament does not pass second reading of bills in faster than two hours, it is too slow and it had better get on with it, have time allocation applied and jam it through in a day.

That is exactly what we have heard from the Minister of State for Privatization this morning: one more day at report stage on this very important piece of legislation that is selling off part of the purchase of Canadian taxpayers, Petro-Canada, which they have bought and paid for with their tax dollars. The government is selling it off in order to meet its lust for privatization of Canada's assets. I submit that the government is misguided, as usual.
Let us hear some more words from the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker who must be held in some esteem by hon. members opposite. I would be the last to want to quote Mr. Diefenbaker as an authority on much, but on the rights of Parliament he had some very sound ideas and certainly he understood the institution better than the present government House leader and his entourage. In fact I would venture to say that Mr. Diefenbaker was one of the best Leaders of the Opposition that Canada ever had. No one will deny that as a Leader of the Opposition he was outstanding. I do not think anyone will deny that as a Prime Minister he was a disaster. The hon. member for Edmonton East would not deny that.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-84
speechtext: I certainly would. The Conservative Party has abandoned John Diefenbaker.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-84
speechtext:
I am sorry that he thinks he was good. He should join the Conservative Party then, because clearly that is where his ghost remains.
Mr. Diefenbaker spoke about the importance of opposition, and I would like to quote again from this speech. I assume it was a speech given in Parliament by Mr. Diefenbaker, but someone with great foresight published it in this book entitled Those Things We Treasure. It is a collection of speeches, and I commend it for reading to the government House leader and his entourage. I quoted from page 46 of this little work:
The need of a strong Opposition is supported by almost every political writer. Among these is Professor Bassett, who has stated that: "The Opposition is not merely tolerated, but treated as indispensable". He emphasizes the existence of an Opposition as an example of the difference between democracy and autocracy.
Opposition is as necessary to the parliamentary system as is the Cabinet. The two are inseparable. One without the other would mean tyranny or chaos. It is commonplace for all governments to view effective opposition as obstruction and this is a view too often and too lightly taken up by critics outside Parliament. An Opposition that discharges its parliamentary responsibilities properly is bound to appear to those opposed as obstructionist.
Government Orders
The weapon of the Opposition is discussion and argument. If the Opposition stand is not justifiable in the opinion of the people, the people are not slow to show their displeasure.
I could go on, but these are words of a former Leader of the Opposition and a former Prime Minister who understood the role of an opposition in Parliament, who suffered at the hands of an opposition in Parliament because it was an effective opposition.
I submit that this government is afraid to suffer at the hands of this opposition, and that is why it keeps closing off debate on the demerits of the bills that the government is continually bringing before this House. Debate on every contentious bill is closed off. I have already indicated the list of over 20 time allocation or closure motions in this Parliament. Never before has closure been used as often as it has been in this Parliament. Yet the government just carries on as though this was a perfectly normal and perfectly standard procedure. The fact is it does not want to hear the truth about the dreadful bills it is producing.
I want to read one more quotation about the role of an opposition, and I quote again from Mr. Diefenbaker:
Without an Opposition, the administration of the day could and would carry on the task of running the country, but such a situation would be identical with a totalitarian one-party state. Efficiency of administration was claimed by Hitler and Mussolini, but freedom died.
That is exactly what is being trampled out here. It is an effort to stifle criticism, to stifle objection, to stifle the legitimate concerns of the people of Canada as expressed through their elected representatives.
We were not sent here to sit and pass bills willy-nilly. We were sent here so we could offer alternatives, criticize proposals, and educate the public on the damaging effects of government measures. Certainly the damaging effects of many of its measures are becoming readily apparent. One only has to look at the unemployment it has created, the high interest rates it has pushed and established in this country, and the various economic disasters with which it has come up. I do not want to go into those matters in the course of my speech, but I do say that in considering the approach to the public this government has an obligation to listen to the people of Canada, to listen to their representatives in Parliament, and to give us a fair and reasonable opportunity to be heard.

Government Orders
We have had one day on report stage of this bill. There were many amendments moved. There are many more to discuss, but the fact is that we are now being limited to one further day and third reading on a very contentious bill is going to be limited to one day. I call it a disgrace and I call on the government to withdraw this motion.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-84
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, once again I find myself participating in a debate limiting the time of the House for consideration of Bill C-84. We had the same thing, of course, at second reading. We had a total of three days of debate on Bill C-84 at second reading.
I should note perhaps that the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill, the Minister of Privatization and Regulatory Affairs, sent a letter to one of my local newspapers, the Edmonton Journal in which he claimed that in fact there had been four days of consideration by this House of Bill C-84 at second reading. Of course, he neglected to point out that one of those days was taken up with the debate on the time allocation motion so that in fact there were three effective days of debate on Bill C-84 at seconding reading, approval in principle of the scheme to privatize Petro-Canada and thereby to alienate from the Crown assets worth, depending on how we wish to calculate it, somewhere between $2.3 and $6.7 billion.
Having been rushed through this House, like an over-large bride to the altar, the bill wound up in committee. In committee, we had an organization meeting a week before we were to start hearing witnesses. This meant that the witnesses that those of us on the opposition benches did manage to convince the government majority to invite, had a week or less to consider whether or not they could make the time to appear before the committee at the times made available to them by the committee; consider whether or not they had the time to prepare the presentation that would do justice to their beliefs and considerations; and consider therefore whether or not it was even worth-while to make the venture.
I can tell you, Madam Speaker, that several of the witnesses that even the committee in its stingy wisdom decided to invite had to decline because they were unable to make the necessary arrangements at such short notice. Although there was no closure or time allocation in the committee, the effect was the same.
Consideration of the bill in committee was truncated. That too has led to inadequate consideration of this bill.
Ten days were devoted to the study of the bill in committee. They were October 31, November 6, 7, 8, 20, 21, 22, 27, 28 and 29. In those 10 days we heard a total of 11 witnesses, of which all but six were government witnesses. We heard six witnesses representing themselves or groups, including the Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association Inc., the Energy Clean Air Caucus of Alberta Friends of the Earth, an investment counsellor by the name of Mr. Gobert, the Council of Canadians, Professor Hershel Hardin. That is about it; $6.7 billion in assets, six non-government witnesses. That is more than a billion dollars a witness. We rushed them through there.
Now we find ourselves at report stage. Several amendments are being proposed. We have had one day's consideration. After one day's consideration, the government has determined that that is enough. It is time to bring down the axe and move this thing off into the final day of report stage consideration and then one day at third reading. That will be the equivalent from the start of second reading to the conclusion of third reading, with all steps in between including all the days spent in committee, to authorizing that expenditure or that alienation of the assets of $6.7 billion at the rate of roughly $400 million a day. That is big spending. It certainly makes me uncomfortable.
I do not believe that this House and its committee has given anywhere near the careful consideration to the bill that it warrants. It is the largest privatization ever undertaken by the government and ever likely to be undertaken by the government. It means the selling off of the one major Crown asset in what, virtually everyone agrees, is a strategic resource area. It is proposed to be done through a regime that will see the Canadian people recoup nowhere close the full worth of their assets.
Why, Madam Speaker? It cannot be haste, arising from the need to have the legislation itself in place because once the proposed legislation passes third reading in this House, it will go the other place. Most people around here are of the opinion at this point that the other place, being consumed with the matter of the GST, will undertake little or nothing else, while that is being considered. Further, it is expected that that consideration will conclude and the sound and fury will finally subside sometime before Christmas. Do you know what happens then, Madam Speaker? The House prorogues and all things on the Order Paper die.
December 11, 1990

So one of two things is going to happen, Madam Speaker. Either this bill will be stuck in the Senate and die with all the other unfinished business there, in which case what is the point of ramming it through the House? Or the GST fight will continue in the Senate, in which case we have plenty of time in this place to give this bill the full consideration it warrants.
But the government is determined that this massive alienation of the assets of the people of Canada, this turning off of those opportunities which Petro-Canada could represent to the Canadian people in the future, those opportunities to diversify our energy base away from the traditional hydrocarbons of oil and gasoline into far greener pastures, should be accomplished with a haste that is at least unseemly and, in my less charitable moments, I would characterize as obscene.
It is clear that the government is not to be dissuaded from this path. It is clear that, as is the case with most other matters that it has brought before this House, at least in my experience here, it is unshakeably convinced of the near divine wisdom of its proposals and is thus uninterested in consideration of either alternatives or of nagging problems within its own proposals. Presumably it believes them not to exist. But I must tell the government, Madam Speaker, that the Canadian people believe them to exist. The Canadian people can see what is going on in this House, they can see the overweening pride with which the government conducts its business in this place and the Canadian people, in the long run, will not tolerate it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs) and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-84
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to deal, just briefly, with some of the statistics that were being used to indicate that there has been a lot of use of closure and of time allocation. Unfortunately, the member is correct, there have been a number of occasions when these were used. But I think if we look back to the period from 1980 to 1984, there were 25 different times that the government of that time, the Liberals, used time allocation and twice that they used closure.
Government Orders
In the subsequent four years, 1984 to 1988, this government used time allocation on 20 occasions and used closure on two occasions. But there have been, in this last two years, as the member has indicated, an unusual number of occasions when closure and time allocation were used. I think a person has to ask why.
Madam Speaker, it does not take a rocket scientist to figure it out. It is obviously considered by the opposition to be good strategy on their part to force the government to use closure or time allocation because it makes them look strong and they have the appearance of opposing. But the reality is that the government must pass its legislation. The people in this country demand it.
They do not understand why it takes so long for us to move legislation through the House. There are a few other things that people of Canada understand, but it is sometimes difficult to get the opposition to understand.
There is good reason for this bill to be passed now, and I will try to address that.
There has been good coverage through the legislative committee. It did have several days of second reading review. I think this government is fully cognizant of the fact that there are many members in this House who would like to speak to this bill.
In endeavouring to satisfy that demand, because we feel it is a legitimate one, we offered to extend the hours last week. That offer was refused by both opposition parties.
I think that tends to speak a little bit to what I consider the seriousness of their desire to really speak meaningfully to some of this legislation.
I would like to address briefly why it is necessary that we pass the bill now. As the hon. member from Edmonton has indicated, it is the largest privatization in terms of dollars that we have undertaken in Canada. Many members would like to see it delayed, because they actually disagree quite aggressively with privatization.
We heard a number of witnesses in the legislative committee who directly addressed this. They told us as a committee: "Yes, you should get the bill through. You should put the minister in a position where he can deal with those shares as early as possible."

December 11, 1990
Government Orders
One of the witnesses, a financial analyst, termed it as a window of opportunity. The bigger the window we provide PetroCan and the investment community, the better their chances of returning optimum value for those shares to the Canadian taxpayers.
I think that is of great concern not only to the taxpayers but to every member in this House. It is a real window of opportunity. The witness talked about some of the current situations in Canada that we know affect the oil industry. We know it affects the share values.
We all know there is a crisis in the Middle East. Nobody knows exactly what the market response will be to it, but it is critical according to this witness that we set our affairs in order so that PetroCan, the government and the Canadian taxpayers can take maximum advantage of that window of opportunity.
I will keep it very brief, because my colleague has already discussed this. We held nine or ten committee meetings. We heard from 10 or 11 different witnesses and groups. There were a lot more people and we did group them, but we consciously tried to hear those people across Canada who the committee felt it was imperative that we do hear from.
We wanted to hear from people representing the environmental lobby groups, and we did that. We wanted to listen to investment dealers, and we did that. We wanted to get some legislative expertise advising the committee as to the PetroCan legislation, and we did have that.
In fact, we had a couple of visits from experts in that area. The committee desired to hear, and we were able to produce, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who gave excellent testimony to the committee.
We heard from the executive officers of Petro-Cana-da. We heard from two labour groups; one representing the Energy and Chemical Workers Union and the other from the Canadian Labour Congress. We heard from a number of other groups, including the Petro-Canada International Assistant Corporation, the Bureau of Competition, the Commissioner of Official Languages who wanted to express his desire to see the French language provisions stretch further than what the bill allowed and what we were suggesting.
We had other consultants and representation from the Canadian Life & Health Insurance Association who were encouraging us to eliminate some the restrictions that we had on the bill. We resisted that effort.
It was an excellent cross-section that the committee heard. We heard testimony for and against, but most of the evidence against the bill tended to address the concept that Petro-Canada should be used as a policy instrument. They felt that somehow or other to understand and to control any of our resources or any of our major industries, we have to own and control a full cross-section of that industry. The logic escapes me, but it seems to be so obvious to others.
That implies to me that, if we want to understand and control the forest industry, the government should be out there acquiring and owning interest in an integrated forest industry company that controls resources in different parts of Canada. People in the industry and across the country would say we would be insane if we felt that that was the only way we could get a window on the industry.
Another major industry I could mention briefly is the food industry. There is nothing probably more important, except the forest industry in Canada. It would imply that for the government to understand, to know what is going on and to control it, we should be owning large tracks of farms and ranches and food processors. Heaven forbid that we should end up investing in the golden arches across Canada so that we have a window on that industry.
With reference to the witnesses we heard from, the Minister of Energy, for one, spoke to it elaborately. I realize I do not have time to cover it completely. Bill Hopper is another. One of the most interesting witnesses was the former minister who I understand had a part to play in the original creation of Petro-Canada as a government agency, Marc Lalonde. Just recently he was asked if we require Petro-Canada as a window on the industry? His response was: "We have developed in the government in the Department of Energy and the National Energy Board certainly a much greater knowledge about the industry than there was in the sixties and seventies." I could go on.

He covered consumer protection, energy prices, and the public policy role. His answer was: "No, no, no. We do not require PetroCan as a window on the industry or for us to know and understand this industry."
I realize my time is up. We do need to get this bill through. The window of opportunity is now. We have heard from the experts and I look forward to the ensuing debate.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate on time allocation on a very important Canadian bill, one which marks the demise of Petro-Canada in Canada.
I say this because we are debating at present the rights of Parliament to have a debate. My colleague from Kingston and the Islands has already spoken about the time that has been spent in debating this bill. We have not had ample opportunity in my opinion to do away with Petro-Canada.
This government does not care about the rights of Parliament to debate. It does not care about the rights of Canadians, through their parliamentarians, to have a say in the policy of Canada. It was only 10 years ago that the very issue of the election was Petro-Canada and our National Energy Program. Canadians said yes to Petro-Canada at that time.
By using time allocation, the government is beginning to show Canadians why it has made Parliament an useless instrument as far as Canadian policy goes. I think that in this bill there should be an open vote. I think that Canadians should be able to tell their parliamentarians what they want from the government and they do not have that ability. We do not have an ability in the House to have a vote of all the Atlantic members together against an issue that the government may be proposing.
We only have a right to get up in two hours of debate and say that the process is wrong. It is wrong that the government cuts out the debate on such an important national company. It shows the complete disregard that the government has toward any process here in Canada. I would go on to say that it shows that the government is intent on destroying everything that has been made to make us a country called Canada.
Government Orders
In six years of government this Prime Minister has brought forward policies that have ended our ties as Canadians and brought about an adversity in regions that our ancestors in this hallowed place worked hard against. It was to try to make a place called Canada.
Petro-Canada had that very goal. It was brought into force at a time when Canadians needed protection in the oil and gas industry. We still need that protection, but the government says: "No, we will privatize everything or we will get rid of it."
Take the trains, for example. They went east and west, or west and east. We do not have them. Thke Air Canada. The government privatized it. We used to have an airline that was first around the world, first in Canada for service and for safety. What do we find now? We do not have even two airlines that can exist in Canada because the policy of the government has been to go right along with the U.S. and deregulate.
The government has done it in the fishery, a natural resource that is now privatized. To what degree? My colleague from Newfoundland can tell me how much he thinks, but I would venture to guess that the fishery in Canada is probably privatized to about 80 per cent if one took the whole range of fish. The government is forcing our fishermen on the east coast in less than a week to make a decision on the livelihood and the role that their enterprise will play. Boats under 45 and boats over 45 must choose from a package of 100 pages sent out to them last week. They have not seen it before and they must choose by tomorrow as to what will become effective January 1. Of course they are confused, but that is exactly what the government wants-confusion in the west, confusion in Ontario, confusion in Quebec, confusion in the east, and it will govern. It will sell Canada short. That is what is happening in this bill.
Why? The Prime Minister does not come in to answer the questions on that. He will give you a smoke and mirrors discussion on what he sees as the role of Canada.
I think we should be given time to go home over Christmas and the government members should be made to ask their constituents whether they want to see Petro-Canada, the only oil company left in Canada, go to the U.S. We are giving 25 per cent ownership in this bill to foreigners.

Government Orders
We used to have expertise in air. We used to have expertise in oil and gas. We were respected around the world for our policies that made us Canadian, from east to west, north and south. But we had a goal as Canadians. The government is tearing that goal apart.
In the east we do not know where we will be after June 1990 because this Prime Minister does not want to give us any direction as to where he wants to see Canada go. He wants to see everything gone. He wants to see his big friends in the United States take it over, just like Petro-Canada and just like what is going to happen to our airline industry, in the end, with a minister who will bring in open skies that will go north-south instead of east-west or west-east-north-south within Canada. This government is tearing everything apart.
Let me just repeat that in our process-and it has certainly been shown up in six years-there has been no consultation with the Canadian people. There is no consultation by this government with its big majority to put an onus on the government back-benchers to go home and ask the people if they approve of the policies that are coming forward.
We are going to have so many parties in Canada that it will destroy Canada by making it into small regions instead of a strong federal system that can compete with all countries of the world. We used to be able to compete with all countries in the world. In oil and gas, we had a spot, not because of Mobil or any of the big U.S. multinational companies, but because the government had given Petro-Canada the ability to sit at the same board tables as the multinationals.
But not this government. This government says: "We'll privatize it." It will privatize it at a time when we are going through a potential energy crisis in the Middle East; when we are in a recession so that only the big income earners, who are not here in Canada except for the few millionaires who are friends of the government and for whom it has provided over the period of six years; when Canadians themselves are having increased oil and heating costs on the east coast that are incredible; and when incomes are going down as people are being laid off because of the readjustments that are happening as a result of the free trade agreement. The manufacturing sector is going out the window, just as this government likes to see all its policies go-out the window and down into the United States.
It is time Canadians started to know that every one of us have a constituency office and every one of us should be listening to our constituents. I would offer that every one of us in the House should be telling our constituents the exact position that their member of Parliament feels on a certain bill. If we were honest with the Canadian people and told them what the objectives of this legislation are, we would find a greater result right across Canada in terms of a bill such as this and in terms of a cut-off on such an important issue as a natural resource that is ours in Canada.
This government does not care about resources. It says: "Whoever is the highest bidder, we will give it to them, as long as they are our friends. If they are not our friends, we will give it to the second bidder. But we are not going to look much further than that."
In the two years that I have been back, I have seen it in the Post Office; I have seen it in the CBC, and I blame the CBC to a certain extent for some of their own cutbacks- I have seen it in Air Canada; I have seen in it with the trains; I have seen it in the fishery which is at our door-step. The government cares nothing about the policy as long as it can privatize a resource.
I know my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I feel very strongly about a time allocation that the people of Canada will not have an opportunity to voice their concerns because their members of Parliament are perhaps not even explaining it to them.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate this morning with regard to Bill C-84 and the privatization of Petro-Canada.
I also had the opportunity of being a member of the legislative committee that reviewed the bill clause by clause. Indeed, we heard from quite a number of witnesses.
What I would like to bring to your attention today, and to indeed the attention of all my colleagues in the House, is that we had about 35 names of witnesses that were proposed from all the members on the committee, which we reviewed very carefully.

We did submit invitations to many of those witnesses. It was unfortunate that some could not come, or were unable to come for reasons which I will not refer to today. Out of the group, we did hear from nine. It was quite a balanced group.
There were some who were very much against the privatization, and I would like to review some of the reasons that they felt the company should remain in control of the government. Of course, there were some witnesses who were for the privatization.
I happen to come from Calgary which is in Alberta and happens to be one of the main producing provinces with regard to fossil fuels, mainly oil and gas. I guess we could say that 90 per cent of our oil and gas does come from the province of Alberta. We are particularly concerned that the total petroleum industry in general is a very healthy one and one that runs with no government intervention.
I speak of no government intervention. Let me clarify that the environment is very important. As we heard earlier-about an hour ago-the Minister of the Environment brought forth the green plan, and I have to commend him for it. Obviously fossil fuels in the emissions are problems.
No matter if the company is a Crown owned corporation or, indeed, if it is a privately owned corporation, it is going to be subjected to the same rulings, constrictions, hearings, observations, criteria and laws of the country.
Whether it is a Crown corporation or private, it will not make any difference. That was one particular issue that was brought forth with regard to the committee hearings.
In another area, it was mainly the fact of security of supply and a Crown corporation could guarantee security of supply. Actually, it is quite the reverse. A Crown corporation cannot guarantee security of supply. The one thing that is so very important is the capital that is needed to explore, develop and produce the hydrocarbons.
It is very expensive, more so with the synthetic type of oils, oil sands and, of course, in our frontiers it is more expensive than the western sedimentary basin.
Aside from that, the fact is that security of supply depends upon the petroleum companies exploring, de-
Govemment Orders
veloping and producing. Petro-Canada presently is quite strapped for funds, and a privatized company would really enable them access to financial markets.
In that case, it is going to make them directly more competitive with the industry. They are going to be able to become more aggressive in pursuing business opportunities.
I know it is hard for some people on the other side to understand, but just one little small word of wisdom is that these companies are in the business to sell oil and gas. When a barrel of oil or an MCF of gas is sold, it has to be replaced.
In order to replace it, a great deal of capital is required. What we are doing here, after a great deal of consultation, is allowing Petro-Canada the freedom to go out and access the capital. We are certainly cutting the apron strings to the government with regard to the financing.
That is not really new, because its mandate was changed in 1985 when it was told to operate within the private industry with no more government funding.
For security of supply, it has a far greater opportunity. With regard to the environment, it will be subjected to the same rules and regulations. I heard an hon. member just a few moments ago speak about Canada selling itself out. There is nothing further from the truth. In Bill C-84, there are qualifications for foreign ownership at 25 per cent. Indeed, no one person can own more than 10 per cent. So, I think the minister has done an excellent job in maintaining control in Canadian hands.
As to accusations that this government is selling out Canada, nothing could be further from the truth. The open skies project that the hon. member mentioned is not a fait accompli. We are holding consultations across the country on the open skies, as is the U.S. The consultations include people from all industries, labour unions, municipalities, airports and provincial governments. It is through these consultations that the ground rules for negotiations will take place. We have not said that there will be open skies. What we are doing is formulating the basis for negotiations, and if it is not good for Canada it will not go through. There is absolutely no way that we would sell out our industries.

Government Orders
We know in the airline industry that perhaps there is not a level playing field, but do not get the idea that because of a proposal, it is a fait accompli. That is simply not the truth.
In the other area about selling out Canada, I remember in December, 1988, the debates on the other side with the free trade deal. Madam Speaker, you know perfectly well that the free trade deal-and it is actually better management trade with the United States-is probably the greatest thing this country has.
We have watched over the last few weeks as the negotiations at GATT failed because of the high subsidies coming from the European market. But, what did we hear in December 1988? "Go to the GATT. That is where you should handle your international trade obligations, put all your eggs in one basket". We said: "No deal, we are not putting all our eggs in one basket. We will look to our greatest trading partner, which happens to be south of the border and you will live to see the day that this country and all Canadians will be grateful that we do have a Canada-U.S. trade agreement".
Not only that, but as the Europeans gather together in 1992 to form a trading bloc, you will see the western hemisphere pull together. When you put 400 million people with the 300 million people in North America, that is 700 million people to compete with the 350 million in Europe.
Let us get back to PetroCan, because it is really what we are debating today. I have to say that the prices of gasoline, oil and natural gas have nothing to do with this government or this bill. We have moved to a free market system, which is exactly the way it should be. If the price of petroleum in the free market goes up, the price of Canadian petroleum goes up. If the price in the free market system goes down, Canadian prices go down.
There is one thing I would like to see, and hopefully it may come about through the petroleum industry. This is the change of price at the pump. It is really relatively slow, but in some other countries it is last in, first out. This means that you see the price rise immediately and consumers may better understand why gasoline prices are going up and down. Right now, we have a 60 day to 90 day lag with the oil that is in the pipeline. So, the reflection of price changes are not seen at the pump for 60 to 90 days, and that is difficult for some Canadians to understand.
Moving to a free market system and a freed up privatized Petro-Canada will enable the company to compete and, after all, what this government is based upon is private enterprise. We should certainly not be holding oil companies under government intervention with regard to expanding their industry.
I am very pleased to participate and want to conclude by saying that we heard from many witnesses on both sides of the question in committee. I feel there has been a very fair hearing and it is time to get on with debate.

Madam Speaker, as the hon. member from the government side was speaking and saying that there has not really been that great a change in Canada with the government's policy relating to Crown corporations, I was thinking about any number of communities, say, Grand Falls, Windsor, Botwood, or Gander, Newfoundland, and about a person sitting at home, right now, in one of those smaller communities and about what that person is thinking.
Well, the first thing that comes to mind about Crown corporations, since this government took over, is that the government sold the telephone company. It sold Terra Nova Tel. Now, when he picks up the telephone to make a telephone call, it is no longer a federal Crown corporation that he is dealing with. He is no longer dealing with "Information" or an operator who might be just next door. That Crown corporation was sold. This person looks down the street, while he is using his telephone, and he sees the place where the post office used to be. This is another Crown corporation and it has been replaced by an outdoor mailbox that he tries to get open when the weather turns cold. The government now sends around the names of various de-icing fluids and there is a hotline; it is nice that he has a hotline in the middle of the winter, to phone if the de-icing fluid does not work on his mailbox. There is 24-hour service and if he phones that number, somebody comes and opens his mailbox.
So the telephone company, a Crown corporation, has been sold. The post office, another Crown corporation, is gone; it has been replaced by an outdoor mailbox. Now, Madam Speaker, this same person worked in Bishop's Falls, a short distance away, where the railway used to be. The tracks are now being taken up. This is another Crown corporation which has been taken away since the Government of Canada came out with its policies on Crown corporations. He no longer can look up into the

sky and see Air Canada planes flying; that Crown corporation is also gone from his airport of Gander.
As if that were not enough, when it comes to his telephone, that Crown corporation was sold by this government, when it comes to his mail, that Crown corporation has a new policy which means no more post offices, and when it comes to getting to his place of work, the railway has been literally taken up and the tracks have been all stacked, just outside of Botwood, with the railway ties also being taken up. Air Canada is gone from his community. Now that was not enough.
There is only one Crown corporation left that Newfoundlanders now deal with and that is the great job-creator in Hibernia, Petro-Canada. Now we have a bill before the House to sell Petro-Canada. So that is his telephone, his mail, the railway, the airline, and his place of work, gone.
There is only one thing which one can conclude from all of that. With all of those Crown corporations gone, there is one more thing that has to go. That is the Government of Canada, and it is going to be gone in the next election.

Madam Speaker, I must say that if you listen carefully these days-and it does not matter what part of Canada you listen to-you will hear a rumbling going on which people ought to know is the government's effort at a demolition attempt to destroy the country.
What has happened is that slowly but very systematically the Government of Canada is dismantling what Canadians understand and know as their country. There is a growing rage across Canada. It does not matter if you are from British Columbia, Newfoundland, or the Territories; Canadians knows that their country is eroding around them.
They know that one of the most effective ways the government has employed to destroy Canada, or as some people have put it to Americanize Canada, is to eliminate those structures and those institutions that have made Canada different from the United States, that have set us apart, that have been uniquely Canadian.
Government Orders
I am talking about the systematic dismantling of the Canadian airline system through the selling off of Air Canada, the removal and elimination of VIA Rail service through critical parts of Canada, the elimination of rural post offices throughout the country, and the dismantling of CBC. We find today in terms of those people who were in hiding in Kuwait that one of the elements which kept their spirits up and motivated them to hope was listening to CBC International. That, of course, will no longer be with us after April 1. The Canadian presence globally through CBC will be dismantled.
We have seen whole sets of Canadian institutions destroyed, eliminated, curtailed, cut back as a result of this government's systematic sort of methodical dismemberment and dismantling of Canada. That is why when people today are asked, "What do you think of the present Mulroney government", they laugh. This isn't a government; it is almost some foreign agent at work in terms of dismantling what we built up over the decades.
We find that in the government's rush to eliminate one of the most critical institutions in terms of differentiating Canada from other countries as a major oil producer, almost every other oil producing country in the world has a national oil company like Petro-Canada. In some countries, as in the Middle East, their Crown corporations control all of their oil patch. Other countries control portions of it.
There is hardly any oil producing country in the world that does not have a version of Petro-Canada, and for a good reason. They want their citizens to benefit from this fossil fuel wealth. They want to have an eye on the industry. That is why we introduced Petro-Canada. Unfortunately, once the mandate was created, it did not operate as a lot of people thought it ought to operate in terms of being different than Mobil Oil, Chevron, Shell, or whatever.
Then the Conservatives decided to give it a very specific mandate and said: "Don't operate any differently than any of the private sector corporations". Then of course, Canadians wonder why we have this corporation which operates exactly like Shell Oil operates its companies. Other countries do not do that. Other countries operate their Crown corporations differently, and so they provide a whole range of additional services to their citizens.

December 11, 1990

What do we see? We see the government introducing closure. This government is so used to bringing in closure that it has become a way of life. Closure has now become a regular way of doing business because this government is anti-democratic. It does not believe in a parliamentary system. If you find the traditions and the time honoured approach of Parliament to be a nuisance, what do you do? You use closure and muzzle debate. You do not allow members of your own party to talk. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I must say that one of the more difficult tasks we have here in the House is to listen to the tiresome hyperbole that we have just listened to, talking about dictatorship and tyranny and so forth.
I would like to go back a bit and remind the member for Kamloops that the parliamentary process really begins not with the tabling of legislation here in the House but on the election trail when each one of the parties lays out its platforms and its intentions for a legislative program in the House. That is when we tell people what our agenda is going to be.
One of the traditions we have re-established in this Parliament that our Prime Minister has brought back to this Chamber is that the legislative agenda has a resemblance to what we talked about on the campaign trail, not like his predecessor, Mr. Trudeau, whose parliamentary agenda bore no relationship at all to the election campaign and the sloganeering.
Government Orders
We have brought back the basis of parliamentary democracy in that the campaign ought to introduce the ideas that we would bring forth in the legislative program. The member for Kamloops does not want to pay attention to this. He has a group of people going across Canada talking to Canadians about parliamentary reform. Meanwhile, that party over there frustrates Parliament here in the House by denying the government its legislation.
I was on the McGrath commission with their party representative, the member for Winnipeg-Strathcona. We took a trip to England to talk to members of the mother of Parliaments who said that over there in the election campaign each party has its agenda. They call it a manifesto, and when the party is elected the opposition party says: "Okay, you are now bringing in your manifesto in the form of legislation. You are entitled, on the basis of your election campaign, to your legislation. Provided that your manifesto laid it out and your legislation matches the manifesto, you are entitled to it".
I think members opposite know there is no secret at all across Canada that we have consistently campaigned on the notion that we believe in privatization. That is no secret. I think neither opposition parties will be fooled by any kind of a notion that we did not believe in that. We believe in privatization.
Back in the 1979 government of the right hon. member for Yellowhead, we brought in a program to begin privatizing Petro-Canada. It should not come as a secret or surprise to these people that we would want to do that.
In the United Kingdom, when they want to talk about the legislation resulting from their manifesto, the parties get together in the House of Commons and agree that the government is entitled to table legislation but the opposition is entitled to lay out its philosophy, its ideology, and its opposition. But the government is still entitled to the legislation. They decide how much time should be given to the debate. They decide if it should be four or five or six, not days, not weeks, but hours-five hours for a debate. Debate on the biggest pieces of legislation in the British House of Commons lasts four, five, or six hours.

Government Orders
This member for Kamloops talks about tyranny because he has not had several weeks to debate a bill, even though we have campaigned on it, even though it is an integral part of our philosophy, even though he knew we would want to do this. He does not believe that the government is entitled to its legislation.
I want him to know that this government was not elected to introduce or enact a socialist agenda. His objection to the legislation is that it does not conform to his ideology. He is entitled to his ideology and his beliefs but we were not elected to introduce his ideology. We were elected to introduce and enact ours. Privatization is an integral part of our philosophy and we are entitled to it. As a truly democratically elected majority government, we are entitled to this legislation.
I do not know why he gets so frustrated and why he introduces all the hyperbole, as did my friend from Gander, "Where is Air Canada gone?" I went home last Thursday and my boarding card said "Air Canada" on it. It had the famous red and white colours. I think all the personnel were Air Canada personnel. I think Air Canada is still flying. Why is it any less Air Canada that there are private shares held rather than public? I think Air Canada is there.
By the way, he says, "Where is the post office corporation?" I believe it was the Liberal Party, the Liberal government that privatized and made that a Crown corporation, took it out of the government portfolio and made a Crown corporation out of it. I think it was Andre Ouellet, as a matter of fact, who did it. Now he says, "Where are all the post offices?" I think they are still there. They have not been taken away.
We believe in this. We believe that privatizing Petro-Canada is good for Canada. I remember when the original bill was first brought in. My friend across the way who represents the farming community remembers when it was brought in. It was supposed to be a window on industry. I think the initial capital infusion was $500,000 back in about 1975. That was the window on the industry. Now we are talking about $5 to $6 billion. Some window. We think that privatizing Petro-Canada will be good for the company and it will be good for Canada.
My friend from Calgary who spoke just a few minutes ago pointed out one of the very important needs of Petro-Canada, and that is a cash infusion. We cannot keep injecting new government capital into that corporation. The people of Canada now know that the government-

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-84
speechtext:
The member for South West Nova says they do not need money. Tell Bill Hopper they do not need the money. They need the money. However, if we do privatize it, if we allow the people of Canada to buy shares, there will be a fresh infusion of cash into that corporation that it could not get any other way.
I want to ask members opposite a very simple question. What is it that creates this marvellous transformation of a company that if it is a Crown corporation, a government-owned corporation, what is it that creates this great transformation of humanity that makes it so much better if the management of the corporation are all of a sudden government employees? Why are government employees running a corporation so much better than private employees who are subject to a board of directors elected by the company, by the shareholders? What is it that makes the president or the board of directors of a government-owned corporation so much more humane, so much more imaginative, so much more generous than if it were a privately-owned corporation?
Does some magical thing take place when that person takes his orders from the government? Would it not be better to have a company like this removed from the government agenda and let it run its own agenda based on the marketplace, without political input, or in some cases political interference?
Would it not be better to have it market driven and let its agenda be driven by the marketplace rather than by an agenda of a political party, whatever political party is in office? Would it not be a more wholesome company if it were driven that way, rather than by the agenda of some people who are elected and have their own agendas rather than a market driven agenda?
December 11, 1990

I say to hon. members that we have been elected on an agenda of a marketplace economy. I have made that freely known in every campaign I have run in and I have run in five. We have always made that known. We are bringing in a legislative agenda on the basis of our political campaign.
The government is entitled to its legislation. The opposition is entitled to voice its opposition. It has no business frustrating it and forcing the government to bring in time allocation.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-84
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate concerning time allocation on this bill.
I have listened with great interest to the speakers. There was an indication that somehow debate is being stifled in this particular matter. The record shows that there have been four days for second reading and approval in principle of this particular bill. There were 18 speakers, nine of whom were opposition members.
The legislative committee held nine meetings and heard from 11 witnesses, as we heard previously. Obviously, nine amendments were also discussed there. There was an opportunity to discuss the various aspects of this bill. Currently, at report stage, there have been 18 speakers; 15 of whom were opposition members.
We have gone through a process, and we will continue to go through a process with regard to this particular bill. There certainly is no intent on the part of the government not to have an orderly debate. Also, the government has the responsibility to get its legislation through and make sure that it is passed.
I look at the particular bill itself, the privatization of Petro-Canada. There has been mention made in the House about the privatization and a comparison made to Air Canada. I had the opportunity on Thursday last to be in Montreal when Air Canada appeared before a committee euphemistically known as the open skies committee.
It was a treat to see a company which is dynamic, ready to approach the problems that will result and the opportunities that will be presented a company that has private shareholders, that feels that it can compete in any market and wants the opportunity to take part in that competition.
Government Orders
There was some reference to certain conditions that they would like to see put forward so that they could compete more adequately in the United States market. They were not unreasonable requests, but they came before us and said: "Yes, we want the opportunity to compete. We feel that we can do it. We feel that we are a vibrant, alive company and we just want the opportunity to be able to compete in any market."
That is encouraging to see. It is not a company holding back, saying: "We cannot take chances. We cannot take part in these opportunities that present themselves." We know that with the globalization of the world markets, more and more competition is coming to the fore. These companies are going to have to be able to respond to that competition.
In that regard, the bill before us will take Petro-Canada into a private situation with private investors throughout Canada. It will give these investors the opportunity to invest in a vibrant Canadian company.
There has been mention about the dismantling of Petro-Canada. Nothing could be further from the reality of privatization. Privatization allows an infusion of capital into these companies. It takes it off the backs of the taxpayers to provide the extra capital that may be necessaiy.
We know the financial position of the federal government at the present time. This privatization is a benefit to the federal government as well as a definite benefit to the company itself. It is better able to compete. It can have a fresh infusion of capital and it can go on and do the things it was set up to do. There will be no dismantling of this company as has been alluded to here, certainly just the opposite.
When we look at the original intent of setting up Petro-Canada as a Crown corporation, we must ask: Is the public policy initiative for this company still necessary? Should it be in a government controlled situation? I would submit that it certainly is not.
The original intent was to increase petroleum supplies and Canadian presence in the industry. Well, Madam Speaker, that has occurred. We moved from an interventionist aspect to one that allows market forces to freely take part and to allow the company to take advantage of the opportunities that present themselves.

Government Orders
We have to realize that the world has changed since Petro-Canada was originally set up. It has fulfilled its function, but it can fulfil its function better as a private company. As I mentioned, with the infusion of private capital and the board of directors being responsible for the company, that will occur.
Petro-Canada was also to act as an agent in any state to state trading. Apparently there has only been one contract ever signed, and that aspect has gone by the board over the years. So that particular public policy aspect for the company has disappeared as well.
We now get to what is the final matter. As has been mentioned, the company was to serve as a window on the energy industry. We have the various boards in place now that can monitor the energy industry, that can look into it. Obviously this is an expensive instrument to use as a window on the energy industry.
Petro-Canada has outlived all of its public policy purposes. With the necessity for an infusion of new capital and the flexibility that will bring when it is privatized, obviously it is important that this legislation get through this House and become law. This is what we are talking about with the time allocation motion.
There is also a question of time. This bill gives the minister, or whomever is designated, the opportunity to market the shares of Petro-Canada. Obviously, that has to be something that is looked at and done in a very timely fashion.
There are a number of safeguards built into the sale of shares. No one individual can own 10 per cent or more of the shares of the corporation. No foreign ownership can exceed 25 per cent. We have discussed that as well when the bill concerning Air Canada was before the House.
This is an opportunity for this company to go forward, to be able to compete and to still fulfil all the public policy objectives that were originally set out. It also unburdens the public treasury from any responsibility that it would have in that particular regard. That is very important in these economic times.
It is a very important bill. It is a bill that should go through this House and obviously is the reason for the time allocation motion that we see in front of us.
It has also been mentioned that maybe the Middle East crisis is going to create some difficulty with security of supply. As I mentioned, the whole world is coming to globalization and a market economy. We see that even in eastern Europe when they realized the futility of trying to have a centralized system and trying to control all aspects of what goes on within their companies. They realize that it has been a failure. It has not worked. They must allow the market to take part.
I see that you are indicating that my time is up, Madam Speaker. Again, with the safeguards that are built into this particular bill, with the opportunity for this company to have an infusion of capital and an independent board of directors, and the opportunity to go ahead in the petroleum industry, it is too important a bill to be bogged down in procedure in the House of Commons. There has been sufficient debate and we will have more. I certainly hope that this bill will go forward.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-84
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today in opposition to the government's decision to invoke time allocation on a bill which certainly affects the lives of Canadians across the country. Why the government does not want a full and healthy debate on the bill is obvious.
I certainly would like to have had the opportunity to voice my concerns in detail on the privatization of Petro-Canada because this bill is a very complicated and detailed bill. This time allocation is denying me the opportunity to discuss in detail how the privatization of Petro-Canada will affect Canadians.
As my colleague suggested in committee, this bill as written states that Petro-Canada may not sell all or substantially all of either its upstream or downstream assets to any one person or group of associated persons. The question is how is "substantially all" defined. That depends on one's view of this definition. It may well be that medium-sized assets that are of national or strategic importance are being left unprotected by the vague wording of this bill. These assets may lose their commercial importance to Petro-Canada but their sale may well impact on the lives of Canadians across our country.

My riding of Malpeque on Prince Edward Island is a rural riding. Such decisions which may not appear to be substantial can really have a major impact on a small community. Such a decision was certainly made by this government when it closed our CFB Summerside. It may not have been a substantial decision when one looks at the enormity of the Government of Canada as a whole, but it had a substantial effect on the lives of many of us in Prince Edward Island. In fact, the after shocks of that decision are still being felt today.
Just last week when I returned to my riding, islanders were concerned about a decision that had been made by Holland College to discontinue adult education classes at Summerside and Kensington as of January, 1991. These classes had to be cancelled due to a shortage of funds. That shortage of funds is really due to two decisions made by the federal government. The first was the closing of the base. Because of that closure, a number of islanders, in an attempt to put their lives back together, enrolled in the Holland College adult education courses to better prepare themselves for finding a new job. This larger enrollment created an under-funding situation.
The second reason was the government's decision to cut back on the funding to the provinces for education. That also of course contributed to the shortage of available funds. Fortunately, the provincial government came to the rescue and provided the extra funding needed to keep these important educational courses alive in 1991. I commend the Ghiz government for its swift and timely action on this matter.
I also commend the students for having the courage and initiative to go back to school to upgrade their skills and knowledge. But, I certainly condemn this government for its policies which created this crisis in the first place.
I condemn the government today for imposing time allocation and so denying me an opportunity to speak in detail about the effects that this bill will have on Canadians, especially Canadians in eastern Canada.
In my province of Prince Edward Island, as in all provinces in eastern Canada, we are very dependent on imported oil. The continuity of supply of this non-renewable resource is paramount to our economic growth and
Government Orders
prosperity. Across Canada, the energy demand for petroleum is about 41 per cent, which certainly is a significant figure. However, in Prince Edward Island, we are doubly dependent upon petroleum for a total of 75 per cent of our energy demand.
We are trying to diversify the energy mix in my province through efforts in such areas as the biomass energy field which involves the burning of wood chips at very high temperatures. This initiative has provided the Island with an environmentally friendly energy source, along with badly needed jobs. Unfortunately, these efforts have been frustrated by the government's cuts to alternative energy and conservation programs. This is yet another example of the government's complete lack of attention to my province of Prince Edward Island. This bill may very well place Prince Edward Island in an even more volatile economic position due to our dependency on imported petroleum.
I urge the government to consider the ramifications of its decisions on the real people out there. There is more to effective decision-making than simply adhering to the bottom line. This bill requires a thorough and full debate due to the complexity of the subject matter itself.
This morning I expected that we in the opposition would have an opportunity to address the concerns of our constituents, concerns that the government is ignoring and which the government is not allowing to be heard in detail in this Chamber.
It is no wonder that Canadians have lost confidence in this government. I certainly regret not having the opportunity to speak in full detail today on the privatization of Petro-Canada.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-84
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I cannot say I am pleased with having to speak on time allocation today, but I want the opportunity to do so because I think that we are faced here with an approach by the government to push through the privatization process of Petro-Canada as quickly as possible. It recognizes that there is a growing wave of discontent across the country relative, not only to this particular bill, but to many other government actions.
This bill is the largest privatization in the history of this government or any other government and covers assets of $6.7 billion on which it will take a loss. There is no way that, under the structure that is being established in this bill, it will get this amount back.

If we had a concern for Canada's well-being, or if this government had a concern for Canada's well-being, it would be sure that there was ample opportunity to discuss the pros and cons of this bill before we got rid of Petro-Canada.
The resource that we are exploiting in Canada, the oil that is being exploited by Petro-Canada and other private corporations, does not belong to those corporations. It belongs to the people of Canada. It should be exploited in the best interests of the people of Canada.
We do not believe-many people of Canada do not believe-that Shell, Esso, Standard, and all the multinational oil companies that do this exploiting are doing so in the best interests of the people of Canada. They do not believe that getting rid of Petro-Canada is the best way to have at least some inkling into what is there.
We recognize that Petro-Canada has, to some extent, ceased to be an instrument of public policy. But this also is a planned approach on behalf of this government.
This company which has a good solid commercial base and more assets than most other companies do have in Canada has not showed up as being as possible as Shell or Imperial because the government has made it a policy approach that it should not show up as being entirely competitive with these companies. The only way it could defend the sale of it was if it was not making a return on its investment.
It has not been a particularly good investment, but it is very difficult at this time to say that we should sell this company. Judging whether or not Petro-Canada has some reason for being in the future, as far as the Canadian people are concerned, it is very difficult to say yes or no to that, because we, as legislators, must be sure before we make that kind of a move that what we do is in the best interests of Canada. We have not explored the possibilities. We have not spent the time necessary to do so.
The Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources did a fairly comprehensive study on Petro-Canada. Indeed, in the process, it made the recommendation that the privatization of Petro-Canada not be proceeded with until the federal government has completed the process begun in energy opposites and has articulated an energy policy.
That is why I suggest that we, in this House, as the Parliament of Canada, are proceeding with this bill much too quickly. In fact, I think that the time allocation should be turned around to the extent that the government should withdraw the bill until it knows whether or not it really needs Petro-Canada as an instrument of public policy.
In the six years that it has been responsible for Petro-Canada, the government has failed to use it. It has directly used it as an instrument of public policy, and it has directed Petro-Canada to operate as any other private sector oil company, except that it was not supposed to make any money.
