Government Orders
where they will have to go out and promote better management and better protection of the fisheries habitat than existed before.
With regard to habitat protection in particular I want to make a few comments. The summary of the information and background material provided to the committee by the minister regarding fisheries violations was very interesting in terms of the number of ticketed offences, some of the habitat convictions, what has happened as a result interventions by fisheries officers, and whether in fact there was any follow through. I ran one particular figure by the witnesses who appeared to see how relevant it was, whether it related to their first-hand experience when it came to the fisheries resource.
In 1988 in the Pacific region there were 1,959 convictions, resulting in about $320,000 in fines. Habitat convictions totalled 11.1 asked virtually all the witnesses concerned about habitat protection who appeared before the committee if this reflected in their view the problem that we are having with habitat protection, at least on the west coast. It was a clear no from virtually all of the witnesses. They said there were severe problems that Fisheries and Oceans officers had in a number of areas. In particular, they said that there was a sense within the department that when officers in their field work come across a skidder running across a creek, damaging a stream or whatever, they are reluctant to charge the particular operator. There is a sense that senior Fisheries and Oceans management will not back them up or support them. In fact it may go as far as Ottawa, that there may not be support there to back them up. If they are in fact charged, just exactly what does happen when it gets into the courts? They are slapped on the wrist, given a $100 fine and off they yet there may have been serious damage done.
That became painfully clear when an internal Fisheries and Oceans memo was released to the public which summarized, in the view of this particular Fisheries and Oceans officer, some of the very clear internal problems within the department when it comes to protecting the fisheries resource. I want to read into the record the particular quote from this memo, because it is clear to me that this officer felt strongly enough about the way the department was conducting itself to write to a supervisor to express concern.
I think it is an important message that we heard in committee and that we talked about in report stage. It has to be repeated today. If we are not aware of how important protecting the fisheries resource and habitat is, we must ensure that the department carries through with any of its concerns. I would like to quote from the memo which reads:
We (DFO officials) have determined that DFO friendly
corporations-will enjoy relative immunity from the Fisheries Act.
The memo went on to state:
-it must be appreciated that DFO habitat enforcement has reached an all time high in inconsistency-
The memo went on to state that "it must be appreciated that DFO habitat enforcement has reached an all-time high in inconsistency". The memo states with respect to current violators of the Fisheries Act, that "because of the immunity phenomenon-a large number of violators-are not being properly pursued-It could appear that Alcan-et cetera, are given immunity from the law and we are just after the little guy".
Probably nothing sums up the concerns which people have with the Fisheries Act than that particular paragraph. It should tell this House how important it is that these amendments and this legislation carries through with the kinds of policies and procedures that will ensure our fisheries will be protected.
In fact, even in today's vague plan-not the green plan because it is really lacking in a great deal of specifics. One of the particular parts of the green plan released today talks about the release of the enforcement and compliance document. It is a very important document for this reason, and it was referred to in our committee by witnesses from the West Coast Environmental Law Association.
This document is the operating manual that fisheries officers use in their day-to-day field operations but has yet to see the light of day. We see yet another promise in the green plan to have it released. It is very important that that document see the light of day because it speaks directly to the comments made in this weak memorandum that the fisheries officers do not feel that they have the support in their department to cany out habitat protection work and to ensure that those kinds of provisions are carried forward.

I do not think we should talk about Bill C-74 and about habitat protection without mentioning a particularly sad example where the department and the minister failed to protect the fisheries resource and that is in regard to the Kemano project.
Last week the former minister of the environment from British Columbia made a very clear commitment to environmental assessment hearings conducted into this project, which will have a dramatic impact on the salmon habitat and the Nechako, a major tributary of the Fraser River. Yet it has been exempted from the environmental assessment process. Obviously, the former minister from British Columbia has learned that to fool with the environment is a very dangerous thing. He has now had to resign from cabinet, and who knows what he will go to next.
It is clear that that very important fisheries issue is not going to go away, it will stay in the news in British Columbia and across the country for some time to come. We have had a number of fisheries and oceans scientists who have expressed their concerns and will likely express their concerns further when this whole matter goes back into the courts in the new year. It is a very important issue that we cannot avoid. We have asked the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to conduct a full environmental assessment whenever the premier of British Columbia gets around to appointing a new or an acting minister of the environment. The whole cabinet is probably acting in some capacity or other because there have been so many resignations from the Social Credit government.
I would encourage the current Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to participate, not just with environmental assessment, but if there is to be public hearings. Are those now out the window because of the resignation of the B.C. minister of the environment who is a partner with this government in helping to destroy the Nechako river and reduce the flows on the Fraser?
Speaking specifically of the Fraser River, a major salmon rearing river in British Columbia, and one that all British Columbians are familiar with, it is going to be probably the subject of more debate to come, more work to come and an integral part of what we are talking about in Bill C-74. It comes to ensuring not just a multijurisdictional approach to resolving a lot of the problems around the Fraser River where all the stake holders are involved, the different resource industries and what have
Government Orders
you, but as well in the commitment that we had, which again has very few specifics.
There is no funding commitment on stock rebuilding and protection of the habit base in the green plan, and of course the commitment to following that monitoring compliance and enforcement measures will be increased. That is essentially Bill C-74. It is important that this be done when it relates to the Fraser River because of the importance of that river to the fisheries in British Columbia.
Our caucus, in particular led by the chair of the New Democrat B.C. caucus, the member for Okanagan- Shuswap, has done some excellent work in preparing a report with our views about the importance of the Fraser River from top to bottom. There has been a management plan for the estuary part of the river that has been generally, not universally, seen as a positive approach and one that should be modelled for the entire river.
Our caucus held the only meeting in the upper end of the Fraser River in Prince George, where the Fraser River coming from the east end of my riding is met by the Nechako River coming from the west and starts its flow south. We were the only group to hold meetings in Prince George to talk about the importance of the Fraser River. As well, there are meetings coming up in the interior and a river boat tour of the Fraser River at the lower end itself. The department has produced what I think is a very revealing document that I certainly would be willing to provide to the parliamentary secretary if he is interested. It is a very revealing document about the concerns that the department and officials have about the protection of the habitat on the Fraser river. It is very revealing and perhaps even controversial. It shows the commitment at the field level from the staff. We hope this commitment is going to carry through all the way up to the minister. I hope it is there and I hope that this bill is going to encourage that that happens.
We have said that we support in principle Bill C-74. We were successful in getting two of my amendments through which the government supported. What is more important than that is I know we are going to ensure that we hold the department and the government accountable. If this bill is going through the House and if we are

Government Orders
supporting it, then in supporting it we have to follow up to ensure that the provisions of the legislation are followed and are acted upon and that the commitment to protect the fisheries resource on both coasts is there; that it is there from the field staff, it is there at the departmental level and it is here in the House of Commons and in the Parliament of Canada.

Madam Speaker, I spoke on second reading of this bill. I attended one of the committees when some of the witnesses came before the committee. I feel pretty strongly about this bill, contrary to some of my colleagues who will be speaking in this debate.
I think it is very good to have a bill with the primary aim of protecting fish habitat, as this bill is supposed to do. But I have three areas of major concern about the bill. They are, first, the use of penalties to fishermen, to help conserve and protect the fish stocks. The second concern is about where these revenues, provided for in the bill, are to come from. They will come from those in the inshore fishery because they are in the majority. I will discuss each of these concerns at length.
Third, I do not feel that this bill will be equally applied. This stems from my second concern which is that the inshore fishermen are the ones who will bear the brunt of this particular move by the Minister of Fisheries. When I say that I do not think the penalties will be equally applied, I feel that it should not just be the inshore fishermen who will bear the brunt of this legislation. What about the foreigners who are overfishing? What about the offshore overfishing that has been going on?
I would like to say that, when one starts using penalties to force conservation and protection of the fish stocks, one can only feel that the communications or consultation process of this government has fallen down. It is like everything else, it has fallen down. I say that, because there is inadequate effort, on the part of the Minister of Fisheries and this government to arrive at a process of consultation with the fishermen who are going to be the ones who are going to bear the brunt of what we pass in this House. Certainly, there is overfishing. Certainly, there has been inadequate stock assessment.
The department of fisheries has not had the money or the capabilities in the Scotia Fundy area to assess the stocks. It has not wanted to listen to the fishermen. You could catch any number of fish in the Bay of Fundy this fall and this summer, and yet there was no reassessment of the stocks, no support to the fishermen who were looking to that stock in order to gain their living. There is no attempt by this government to reassess or to come back with an assessment of the stocks, an assessment which the industry has called for, I have asked for in this House, and the local communities have asked for. Madam Speaker, I say that this shows the inadequacy of the fishery policy of both the previous minister and this minister.
I will just read a letter which I received last night from a group of dragger fishermen, who have vessels which are under 45 feet long. I am bringing this up because it just happens that Canada's Green Plan mentions this and I will deal with it shortly. The letter states that, in respect of the individual boat quota allocation, it was agreed by the association not to accept the proposal, as is. This is a plea because these fishermen have to accept this by tomorrow. They say that it was agreed by the association not to accept the proposal as is. They got the proposal last week. It is about 100 pages long. They say: "We feel that the individual boat quota, as proposed, would be very destructive to the conservation of our fish stocks."
They go on: "The individual boat quota proposal does not address the problems of possible large-scale dumping of fish". We know that this goes on; the minister is aware of it; and, the department is aware of it. The letter goes on to say that the "problem of select high-grading is not addressed". Select high-grading means that they will take the larger fish and throw out the others. They will select from their catch and throw the smaller fish out. So it does not address that problem at all.
"It allows for dumping and for transhipping." That means if they have put their nets in and come up with too much, they either dump it in order not to meet the individual quota, or they give it to someone else-transhipping.
The association has said the individual boat quota proposal "does not address the problems of possible large scale dumping of fish, or select high grading which would cause dumping and transhipping which would be to the detriment of fixed gear quotas".
December 11, 1990

At this time, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans does not have the capability to curb the above problems which are sure to have serious consequences on our fish stocks. If it does not have the capability, why are we passing an act that, as I said, allows it to go and apply in an unequal fashion?
The association agreed that "more time was needed to implement a fishing plan that would better serve the fishermen, industry, and communities, again emphasizing better methods for conserving our stocks of fish". This is what this act is supposed to be about. They are asking for consultations.
In determining individual boat quotas, and I am reading again from the letter: "Using history, we feel an injustice has been done." This is the question that the fishermen are asking me, as well as other members of the House, I am sure, who come from inshore communities. Why can the government not listen to the fishermen? It has all this consultation. Why can it not listen to them that such a proposed quota policy is not going to work.
Yet today in Canada's Green Plan, it states at page 76, under "Domestic Action":
Individual quotas, sometimes called "boat quotas" or "enterprise allocations", are an important feature of the management of several Atlantic fisheries, including groundfish and offshore scallop. They are shares of the Total Allowable Catch (TAC), or fleet allocation, assigned to individual licence holders. Individual Transferable Quotas (ITQs) take the approach one step further by allowing transfers among licence holders. This provides greater flexibility and promotes more efficient utilization of fishing capacity. ITQs have been implemented in several domestic fisheries and are in place in other parts of the world, including the fisheries of New Zealand and Australia.
Just on that point, we had Mr. Nichol from the west coast come before the Fisheries Committee recently. He mentioned that 85 per cent of the fishery in New Zealand was now privatized. But the ownership was not in New Zealand. It was with multinationals. It did not belong to New Zealand any more. What was theirs in their waters did not belong to them. It had been privatized because of the individual transferable quotas.
But it is stated in the first fisheries item in the green plan:
Government Orders
Accordingly, in consultation with the fishing industry and the
provinces, the government will put in place a system of Individual
Transferable Quotas (ITQs) for various fisheries.
There are two things in that statement by the Minister of Environment. His counterpart, the Minister of Fisheries wants to see individual transferable quotas in various fisheries. To me, various fisheries could mean the lobster fishery, the crab fishery, or any type of fishery, capelin or whatever.
I have just read from a letter from a person in desperation to the Department of Fisheries saying that it was not consulting. Nobody in the industry wants individual boat quotas. No boat that I know of under 65, wants an individual boat quota without-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: You better check your facts.

My colleague says that I had better check my facts. I can guarantee you that the only ones who want an individual boat quota are the minister's officials. I do not know why they want it. Is it for their rich friends who can then buy those individual transferable quotas, and eventually we will have a multinational company of the fishery on the east coast?
The government uses that example, and then comes back to this act and states that "we are going to use individual boat quotas for conservation and protection of our fish stock." The whole being of this bill before us, Bill C-74, is to conserve and protect fish stock.
It does not make sense when there is a group saying that they would like to consult with the government, giving the things that they would like to see addressed, such as a management plan and consideration of under utilized species 4WS, east of Halifax on the mesh side, size of fish, fuel costs, and gear costs. Those are all good ways of looking at conservation.
With regard to mesh size, for instance, the sector applied a mesh size this year in that area, and it worked. They had been asking the department to put in a mesh size for years, and it worked. We got a good sized fish.
Now, on top of all of this and without any consultation, as of January 1, 1991, we are going to have new regulations that are going to affect every inshore fisherman whether in P.E.I., New Brunswick, or Nova Scotia. The penalties are going up.

December 11, 1990
Government Orders

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: For those who break the law.

The maximum penalties on summary conviction for a first offence-I come to my second point.
The parliamentary secretary over there is hollering at me, but I would say: Where are they getting the revenues?
Let us face it. The bulk of their fishermen are in the inshore. It does not apply to overfishing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: The bulk of them obey the law.

Any good legal person would tell you. Who are the people who cannot afford the lawyers? Who are the people who go in and plead guilty?
There is nothing in this act that separates a small, under 42-foot boat, an under 45-foot boat, an under 65-foot boat, or an over 125-foot boat. There is nothing in this act that distinguishes 1,000 pounds over, 500 pounds over, or 200,000 pounds over, which one might see. There is no distinction.
Because of that, we will find that the ones who can afford a good lawyer will probably get off. I am a lawyer. I know that. If they can afford a good lawyer, they are probably going to get off.
Fancy lawyers.

Fancy lawyers is right.
The bill does not distinguish between a big and a small infraction of the law. It does not say that the big can afford a defence lawyer, and the small are probably going to plead guilty. It does not say that the Department of Fisheries has the discretion to pick and choose whom it is going to go after, because it is overworked.
If it was applied to everybody, then people would say: "Well, everybody is going to get it." But they are not going to apply it to everybody. They are going to go to the easiest port or the easiest harbour and apply it to whomever happens to be there. It might be the one guy who happens to have a few more fish in his boat on that particular day and who never offends a law.
The department does not seem to be able to go after those people who break the law. Most fishermen would say it should go after them. For some reason, those are the people who get away.
As I said, it does not distinguish between the big and the small, between the big companies that can pay penalties and can get the benefits of having maybe thousands of fish over a long period of time-they may be caught once, get a good lawyer and get off-and the fisherman who may have that one catch for the first time over the limit is caught. He probably goes into court scared, and pleads guilty.
As I said, Madam Speaker, this bill does not go after some of the culprits who are out there. We give our under-utilized species away. We give them away. Just like we do not have a stock assessment, we do not have a program that helps the fishermen or the industry get into the under-utilized species. We just give it away and give a bi-catch that the foreigners can overcatch, dump, or select and throw out. We are not going after them.
We are not going after the Americans who come over on the Georges Bank side and take the fish when our fishermen are not allowed there because of stock protection.
This bill has many things in it that are bad for an inshore fishery. I can support the basic concept of protecting the habitat. I can support the oil-liner or the tanker that goes by and cleans out its oil tanks as it is leaving being penalized. That person should be penalized. Maybe there is not enough within the act to penalize that type of destruction of the habitat.
I cannot support a process that is just encouraging the minister not to consult with the industry and not to have letters come here stating that it has not consulted and that it is forcing people to take a ballot tomorrow. There is not one fisherman to whom I have spoken who was pleased with the results of lack of consultation or that whatever they had put forward had not been listened to.
I say to all my constituents who are fishermen, and I feel bad, that they should be aware that this bill will probably pass and be in force on January 1, and that the offences and the penalties are very serious. I say that because I am sure that it will be the inshore again which bears the brunt of this Minister of Fisheries' lack of putting into place a proper management plan that reflects that we have a natural resource. If there is a
December 11, 1990

good assessment of stocks, then there will be fairness in the fishery. There will also be an understanding by the players in that field that once the stocks are taken, then the fisheries should be closed.
This is not the way it is. The government is saying: "We are going to catch you, no matter what you do, whether the stocks are still there or whether the quota has been taken. If you come in that day over the limit, you have had it."
My time is almost up. I cannot say that I can support this bill. Given the opportunity, I will be voting against it. I think it shows policy that has no consultation with the industry, particularly the inshore. Again, the government is privatizing, using fines and penalties to overcome its ability to go out and consult with the people of Canada as to the viability of a natural resource, the fishery.
Hear, hear.

Madam Speaker, as this is my first opportunity, now that the questions and comments are in place, I would like to assure my friends opposite that indeed I will speak in this debate. First, the premise that we must operate under is the people that will be paying penalties or fines under this act are only people who have broken the law of Canada, who have been charged and convicted. They are not the lion's share of my fishermen, and the fishermen whom I know, who do not break the law. They are so concerned about the management of the fishery that they, themselves, take into hand the law to preserve the fishery.
On the question of consultation, and I stand to be corrected, but I do not remember one witness, and I was there for every single one of them, who complained they had not been consulted. Madam Speaker, on October 16, 1989, I rose in the House and put a question to the Minister of Finance on the matter of poverty. The question pointed out that the Vancouver food bank provides 3,200 bags of food weekly; Edmonton's food bank feeds 11,000 people each month; Regina's food bank provides 5,500 meals, and 6,000 boxes of food a month come from Regina's food bank; and Toronto's food bank feeds 84,000 people a week. A Montreal study shows that one in five kids are hungry in this country. Food banks in Canada are becoming institutionalized.
I asked the minister if he was planning to wait until food banks in Canada bar their doors to force this government to act or is the government going to provide adequate financial support for Canada's hungry.
The response was:
-during the course of the last five years we have demonstrated-
We, meaning the government.
- a very dear commitment to addressing the problems of those in lower income brackets.
The minister went on to say:
Let me enumerate some of these matters.
He said, referring to the government again:
We have increased the size of the child tax credit quite
significantly from what it was in 1984. We were the first government
to bring in the refundable sales tax credit. That sales tax credit has
been increased on two occasions since its introduction in 1986.
He also went on to talk about:
-changes that resulted in 850,000 low income Canadians being put in a position where they would not have to pay tax-
So, in each of these three areas he feels that the government has addressed the problems and the cause of poverty in this country.
December 11, 1990

That was on October 16, 1989. Today is December 11, 1990. When I rose last October and raised the question that we are discussing today, there were 906,000 unemployed in Canada. The unemployment rate was 6.7 per cent. Today, the latest figures show that there are
1,246,000	unemployed workers in Canada. The unemployment rate is 9.1 per cent. Since June some 200,000 more have been added to the unemployment lines.
Since the finance minister has finally acknowledged that we are in a recession, he has to address this question in a far more serious and meaningful way than to just say we have introduced tax credits that assist the poor.
First of all, many, many of the poor already are not in a bracket where they are required to pay taxes. This is a recession of the government's making. These figures that I have just given do not fully convey the depth and breadth of hardship faced by hundreds of thousands of Canadians. Too often we talk in terms of numbers. In this case, I will give one more number. In the last year 1.4 million Canadians have depended on food banks to survive. This 1.4 million people represent the fall-out of a made-in-Canada recession, the fall-out of unemployment, and the fall-out of poverty that is becoming deeper and deeper in this country.
We have to look at those families who are visiting the food banks.
We have to look at what the dramatic and difficult realities are in their lives, the reality of going from a family that is in full productivity in terms of being part of the community, a family that has pride and dignity in work, that lives in a home and participates fully in the community, that becomes unemployed or under-employed and, in fact, finds itself living in a situation of poverty, that because of lost employment must move to another home, moves down in terms of the cost of living and in many cases loses their home. Such a family may indeed be in a position now-and many families who are not unemployed during this recession and have been living the recession throughout the period since I raised this question-of having to deny their children full participation even in the school system, in the kinds of things that their peers and classmates need to do, who are not allowed to participate in extracurricular school activities because of poverty. This makes a difference in a child's life. I guess the most important part is that the
Adjournment Debate
increase in demand in food banks is escalating and children in this country are hungry.
As we look forward to going home to join our families for the Christmas season, again we have hundreds of thousands of families in this country who cannot think in terms of Christmas but only getting through one more month until the cheque comes, who must go to a food bank to ensure that their children get the basic necessities. Yet, Canada is a signatory to the UN's commitment to the UN Children's Bill of Rights which states that children shall have a home, shelter, food and an education and, yes, even the right to play. Yet, in Canada 1.4 million Canadians are dependent on food banks to survive.
All estimates point to a dramatic increase in the demand for service and that demand has no place in a country like ours. Four more food banks have opened in Newfoundland. Food banks in Surrey are receiving 200 new applicants a month and a further 100 people a month are being turned away. In Toronto, food is being rationed because of the high demand. One hundred thousand people in metro depend on a food bank each month.
It is no longer acceptable for the minister to get up and tell Canadians that all these jobs have been created because people cannot live on incomes from McDonald's, Kentucky Fried Chicken or service industry jobs. People in Canada need decent paying jobs and they need full employment.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship); Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member has asked if the government is going to provide adequate financial assistance for Canada's hungry. Her question shows quite clearly that she simply does not understand the programs that the government has done and is doing to help the disadvantaged in this country.
The hon. member should know that the federal government actually shares 50 per cent of the provincial expenditures on welfare under the Canada Assistance Plan. It is true that the government has proposed in the last budget that the three richer provinces of Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario be subject to the 5 per cent ceiling under CAP. However, the lower-income provinces are not subject to that ceiling. In those provinces the federal government matches dollar for dollar whatever the province spends.

Adjournment Debate
Under our Constitution, the federal government cannot interfere in an area of provincial responsibility. Responsibility for setting welfare benefits at an adequate level rests with the provinces, and I therefore invite the hon. member to point her finger at the provinces, not at the federal government.
While provinces are responsible for the welfare system in this country, the federal government has indeed not shirked its duty in areas where it does have constitutional responsibility. The government has implemented a number of social initiatives to help those Canadians with low incomes.
One of the first things we did upon coming into office was to extend eligibility for spouses' allowance to all widows aged 60 to 64, and more than 50,000 low-income Canadians, many of them who are women, benefit from this provision.
We have taken steps, in collaboration with the provinces, to help social assistance recipients get off welfare. We are spending some $1.8 billion, as part of the Canadian Jobs Strategy to help people find jobs.
The government has also announced a new human services strategy to help Canadians take advantage of job opportunities. The government has implemented tax initiatives to help low income Canadians. The child tax credit has been increased. The federal sales tax credit was introduced. A new supplement to the credit has been introduced for pre-school children. The credit is now delivered twice a year, which we are very pleased about, and some 850,000 low income Canadians have been dropped from the tax rolls, as a result of tax reform.
The federal government has therefore already acted vigorously to meet the needs of low income Canadians, because Canada must be caring and compassionate to those who cannot help themselves. The federal government is quite prepared to do its fair share.

Madam Speaker, on the previous occasion when I asked the minister why the Toronto backlog office had decided to bring Caribbean backlog claimants to the front of the line, although
they were distinctly the last to come in, mostly just two years ago at the end of the backlog period, I was told that this was not happening.
Some of the evidence that this is happening was presented to some of us today at an informal meeting with some members of the Black Action committee. Some described their experiences as consultants accompanying a client and the client being asked: "Are you from Trinidad? Yes, okay, we will hear you. Are you from Jamaica? Yes, we will hear you. Are you from Iran? Yes, we will hear you another day". This was definitely sorting out people from the Caribbean as against people who had been here years longer.
In fact, in a meeting on September 9 with representatives of the bar association, Mr. Pirie, a senior official of the department of immigration in Ontario, was quite frank and said: "Yes, we have changed the rules three or four times, since the minister said first come first served. We are bringing in the Caribbeans first". Now the reason he gave was because they speak English and they do not need to take time for translation or to find translators.
Partly as a result of that, yes they have increased the rate at which they are reviewing the backlog cases, but they are still going to have to take up those Iranians or Sri Lankans or Salvadorans. It will take just as long to do these cases six months from now as if they took them in the proper order that the minister directed. The department is not speeding it up; it is only manipulating the statistics, in order to look as if it was being speeded up.
In fact, in the two months from the end of July to the end of September the number of cases that was reviewed increased by 20 per cent. For Iranians it was 5.7 per cent, for El Salvadorans it was 4.8 per cent and for Sri Lankans it was 3.6 per cent, all under 6 per cent, but for Trinidadians there was a 197 per cent increase in the number of cases they brought in and for Jamaicans there was a 35 per cent increase. Clearly, the program is not being run the way the minister directed it should be run, the way the minister has said it is being run, both in this House and when she came to meet with the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. This is a very serious matter.

There are three possible explanations as to why they are bringing the Caribbeans first. One is the given one which does not wash because, as I say, it will take them just as long to do them all together when they have done the Iranians and the others who cannot speak English.
Another is that practically all those people are black skinned, more or less black; not white anyway. The minister finds it offensive to suggest that there could be a racial prejudice there. I find it offensive there is evidence of racial discrimination there.
Finally, in fact what Mr. Pirie said is that we are bringing the manifestly unfounded cases first. Contrary to law, Canadian law and the United Nations law, which says that each case will be judged individually if they have claimed refugee status, they are saying that all the Trinidadians are cheaters, all the Jamaicans are cheaters, and "we will whistle them through like that".
Seven Trinidadians have been found by the panel to have a credible basis. By the minister's rules they should be landed. Oh, no. No, the minister has appealed all seven of those Trinidadians cases found to have a credible basis and should be landed, according to the minister's rules.
In other words, the minister does not want it to appear that anybody in Trinidad has a credible basis or a credible claim to refugee status.
I can understand the minister does not have time to sit in hearings rooms and see what is going on. I understand that some of her Ottawa officials have, at best, very little time. But if the minister does not know what is happening in her city-she has a riding just north of me, St. Paul's riding-there are people she can ask, such as reputable lawyers in private practice, some of whom have appeared successfully at the Supreme Court.
This government lauds private enterprise for privatizing all kinds of public industries because private enterprise, according to this government, is the way to go. They regularly condemn lawyers in private enterprise who represent refugee claimants. Most of these refugee claimants have very little money. No lawyer is going to be a millionaire by representing refugees.
Adjournment Debate
Only in refugee law does the government-and I have heard this more than once from officials, from the ministers and from the chairman of the Immigration and Refugee Board-constantly blame private lawyers for slowing down the process. They constantly overlook the adjournments caused because the department has not brought the translator or the case presenting officer or the adjudicator, or does not have a board room for them to meet in.
There are all kinds of delays. It is about half called by the representative of the department and half called, according to their figures, by the representative of the client. Yet the minister and others only talk about the one side. They are too defensive in trying to defend the indefensible. They had better admit the truth of what is going on, even if it is not what the minister directed.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to expand upon the reply given by the hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration to the hon. member for Trinity-Spadina on October 30.
We met earlier this afternoon. In fact we rushed from the meeting here. We probably could have exchanged papers there and saved some time here.
First of all, processing of backlog claims has not been specifically directed toward those from the Caribbean. The ordering principle for processing backlog cases has generally been to deal with the oldest cases first.
As the hon. member knows, claimants from the Caribbean countries form a large part of the backlog population. The time has now come, as everyone knew it would, to process those claimants. Any suggestion that this or any other group has been singled out for special attention is simply wrong.
Although the backlog clearance program was slow to start, in recent months the processing rate has improved considerably. As of October 26, 54 per cent of the backlog of 85,000 cases has been opened and 31 per cent has been decided.
Furthermore, the Toronto backlog office is attempting to maximize operational efficiency by scheduling panel hearings according to language, interpreter availability being considered, background and any other relevant factors.

Adjournment Debate
However, other backlog processing activities continue in the meantime, as does regular immigration program delivery.
It should be noted that backlog processing activities are resourced and staffed separately from the regular immigration process activities. These are temporary resources allocated specifically to deal with the backlog.
To those who want an amnesty or an administrative review, we say that neither is a solution. Canadian experience and that of other countries has demonstrated that such measures simply do not work.
With respect to the new refugee determination system, Bill C-55 is in fact working quite well. Three of the major goals of the new legislation were to reduce the amount of time that it took to render a decision, to render fair and consistent decisions, and to reduce-if not stop-the flow of manifestly unfounded claimants. All of these goals have, to a large extent, been accomplished. There have not been any large scale movements of manifestly unfounded claimants such as was seen with the old system.
There has been some difficulty in moving to maximum efficiency, but this is normal for a new and very complex law. In the first nine months of 1990, 27 per cent more cases were opened than in all of 1989, and 20 per cent more cases were terminated than over the same period the previous year.
While there has been an unfortunate build-up of cases in the system, it must be remembered that cases are being decided in a number of months rather than a number of years, as was the situation under the old system.
The refugee determination system has seen the intake of new claimants almost double in the second year of its operation. Given the results to date, it is apparent that the system is coping quite well with what is coming before it.
The Auditor General has recently proposed a number of changes, and many had already been acted upon. For example, when the Auditor General suggested that steps be taken to reduce the number of adjournments and improve the scheduling of hearings, the department sent out in August, 1990 detailed directives outlining a modified approach which reduces the number of adjournments, and increases the efficiency and effectiveness of scheduling. In December, scheduling supervisors met to
analyze the progress in scheduling and to work out improved procedures to reduce the number of adjournments.
The Auditor General proposed that the first hearing process for cases not contested by the Minister of Employment and Immigration be streamlined. Employment and Immigration undertook two pilot projects in Vancouver and Niagara Falls. It evaluated and simplified the inquiry process, in which all cases conceded that first level hearings would be dealt with by means of a paper process only. Following these pilots, Employment and Immigration moved to implement the process nationally. This is being done right now.
Finally, the Auditor General stated that Employment and Immigration should consider having medical examinations and security and criminality checks conducted promptly following the time a person claims refugee status, given the high percentage of acceptance experienced to date. Procedures are in place to conduct criminal checks on persons arriving at ports of entry whose identity is in doubt. Efforts will be made to speed up medical and security checks.

Madam Speaker, to follow up on numerous earlier questions to the Minister of Transport, I would like to take this opportunity to reflect on the conduct of Burlington realtor, Peter Lush, in his conflicting roles as Chairman of the Hamilton Harbour Commission and agent for the vendor of pieces of property the Hamilton Harbour Commission was interested in purchasing. Most importantly, I would like to summarize the government's actions which perpetuated the conflict.
Realtor Peter Lush, who resigned his position with the Harbour Commission on October 2 of this year, was initially appointed to the Hamilton Harbour Commission in December of 1986, and subsequently re-appointed in 1989 by Orders in Council.
It was widely known that Mr. Lush had several close friends in cabinet, such as the Conservative member for Lincoln, who, it is reported, encouraged and supported Mr. Lush into becoming chairman.
It is also known that, at the time of his appointment to the Harbour Commission, Mr. Lush declared that he would not have become a harbour commissioner if it meant giving up his real estate listings with J.I. Case that

the Harbour Commission was interested in purchasing. However, the appointment was made anyway, despite the conflict of interest that would have been glaringly apparent to all in 1986 when the present Deputy Prime Minister, in his capacity then as Minister of Transport, made the appointment. Mr. Lush had to swear an oath in relation to the Hamilton Harbour Commission's policy guidelines. The objective of the guidelines are clear:
The object of this policy is to conserve and enhance public confidence in the integrity of the Hamilton Harbour Commissioners by establishing clear rules of conduct respecting conflict of interest and to minimize the possibility of conflicts arising between private interests and the public duties conferred upon commissioners."
Not only were sections of the policy breached by Mr. Lush, but the objectives stated above were not even considered by Mr. Lush until three years after his appointment, and only then because the matter was raised in this House. However, his business associations in connection with the harbour commission should have been dropped at the outset of his appointment, as is prescribed in the conflict guidelines. Guideline (d) provides that: "On appointment to office, Commissioners shall arrange their private affairs in a manner that will prevent real, potential or apparent conflicts of interest from arising." In short, Mr. Lush should have either given up those listings that the harbour commission was interested in and for which he was the broker, or Mr. Lush should not have accepted the appointment in the first place.
The law firm engaged to report on the conduct of Mr. Lush, commissioned by this government, reported to the minister in connection to this very point:
In order to comply with guideline (d), Mr. Lush had an obligation to arrange to have Lush Realty Corp. cease acting as the vendor's agent for J.I. Case, in its dealings with the Hamilton Harbour Commissioners as soon as he took office as a commissioner in January, 1987, and not over three years later on March 13, 1990. Mr. Lush did not, by simply declaring his interest and abstaining from decisions, avoid or withdraw from the situation that was giving rise to the conflict. By continuing to have his company act as agent for J.I. Case, he was in a position of constant and continuing conflict.
Mr. Lush advised the Minister of Transport on March 13, 1990 of his decision to dissociate his group of companies with J.I. Case lands in Hamilton, which he
Adjournment Debate
should have done much sooner. However, evidence has shown that Mr. Lush did not sever those ties. Notwithstanding, it was convenient for him to declare a dissociation because the final deal on the $10 million property in question was made on March 9, 1990, just four days earlier.
During those crucial days, I drew to the attention of the Minister of Transport that Mr. Lush was in a continuing conflict of interest in his capacity as Chairman of the Hamilton Harbour Commission. The minister merely challenged me to make my allegations outside of this House, which I eventually did, but he did not address the substance of my concerns. The minister said that there was an allegation made at an earlier time, which was vetted by the counsel for the Hamilton Harbour Commission.
I would like to know how two so diametrically opposed and dissimilar reports could have been issued with regard to the affairs of Peter Lush. The first report into the affairs of Mr. Lush came as a result of one of the commissioners requesting the commission's lawyers to give an opinion as to Mr. Lush's position.
The law firm noted that Mr. Lush was in a conflict of interest, but that he had declared so and refrained from decisions with respect to the properties as a commissioner. The firm also noted that with respect to section (j) of the policy guidelines, that "a commissioner should not -enter directly or indirectly into a transaction of a pecuniary nature either with himself or any other member of the commission", and that, "purchase of land by the commission was not a transaction of a pecuniary nature with Mr. Lush, either directly, or indirectly. The transaction is with J.I. Case, and while Mr. Lush will clearly benefit from the purchase, he is not a party either directly or indirectly to the purchase of the land."
Subsequently, after I asked numerous questions in the House last March, the harbour commission again consulted its lawyers in regards to those accusations and was given the same opinion.
The most recent legal opinion of November 5, 1990, goes completely contrary to the advice given to the harbour commission in 1989. The law firm which the Minister of Transport commissioned set out the conflict in precise terms:

Adjournment Debate
There can be no question that in the negotiations for the sale of lands, the interests of J.I. Case, represented by Lush Reality Corp., were in conflict with those of the Hamilton Harbour Commissioners. J.I. Case naturally wished to sell its lands at the highest prices and on terms most favourable to it. The Hamilton Harbour Commissioner, on the other hand, wanted to buy the lands at the lowest possible prices and on the terms most advantageous to them.
That is the crux of the problem, Madam Speaker. To whom does Mr. Lush owe a greater allegiance? To whom shall he act in the best interests?
Obviously, that was a dilemma of which Mr. Lush did not rid himself, and when I pointed it out to the Minister of Transport, he scoffed. The minister should have known, as a lawyer and former Attorney General of Canada, that it was impossible for Mr. Lush to carry out his public duty when, on the one hand, he stood to gain financially by his position and, on the other hand, he could not have acted in the best interests of the Hamilton Harbour Commission.
The law firm concluded on this point:
-the commissions to be paid to Lush Realty Corp-were to be a percentage of the ultimate purchasing prices. It was, therefore, in the interests of Mr. Lush to reach agreements for the sale of the lands at the highest possible prices. This put his personal interests- in direct conflict with the interests of the Hamilton Harbour Commissioners.
I submit in conclusion, Madam Speaker, that first and foremost the government and the Minister of Transport are responsible for their actions as the appointees, whether they like it or not. The government must make every effort to reclaim over half a million dollars paid to Mr. Lush since those moneys were ill-gained.
Second, I conclude by sa^ng that there must be a better way to ensure that this type of activity does not happen again, including remedies for wrongdoing that result in the termination of the appointment, and if the wrongdoing involves monetary gain that the moneys must be reclaimed.
Finally, if a request is made by a public body to their counsel requesting an opinion as to a conflict of interest by any of their officers, that the opinion be submitted to the Governor in Council for a second reference to ensure government and ministerial accountability.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to say for the record that this government, under the leadership of
the Prime Minister, in September, 1985 brought in the most comprehensive conflict of interest and post-employment code for public office holders ever brought forward by any Canadian government. The aim of that code was to ensure that public office holders conform to a number of principles that would ensure the integrity, objectivity, and impartiality of government agencies.
As with any new ground-breaking initiative of this nature, the process and application were put forth without complete benefit of past experience.
As we all know, with the benefit of hindsight our decisions would be a lot easier to make. However, with some experience in the field now, we have a greater understanding of the inherent difficulties that are encountered in the day-to-day application of the conflict of interest guidelines. The guidelines are meant to provide a balance between the need to enlist the assistance of competent and experienced appointees to government agencies and the need for those agencies to live up to the highest standard of public scrutiny.
If the criteria were to be so stringent as to exclude anyone with outside business interests, you would agree that we would be hard-pressed to find qualified individuals to sit on many government agencies, boards and commissions.
When Mr. Lush was reappointed on December 16, 1989 to the Hamilton Harbour Commission, all parties were aware of his business interests. During the time of negotiations for the purchase of the parcel of land from J. I. Case by the Hamilton Harbour Commissioners, Mr. Lush declared his conflict of interest in accordance with the commission's conflict of interest guidelines and was not a party to the ratification of the purchase and was absent from all commission discussions pertaining to the transaction.
Notwithstanding previous legal opinions which stated that there was no conflict, when the minister became aware of the situation in March, 1990, as the hon. member opposite has alluded to, he immediately moved to ensure a severance of Mr. Lush's interests in the land dealings and was assured this had happened.
The hon. member opposite professed himself to be satisfied with the action taken.
I believed it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
When the issue was raised again in October and the minister became aware that there may not have been total severance, he requested and received the resignation of the Chairman of the Hamilton Harbour Commission, Mr. Peter Lush.
With respect to the question raised by the hon. member, the minister gave his word to this House that a thorough and impartial review of the facts would be carried out, and he kept his promise. The law firm that conducted the review submitted its report and in accordance with the commitment made to this House by the minister, the report was made available to the public. In addition, the minister has written to the heads of all federal agencies that report to him and asked them to review the opinion of the independent law firm and to bring it to the attention of all persons subject to the
Adjournment Debate
conflict of interest guidelines in their respective agencies.
Furthermore, the Harbour Commissions have also been instructed to seek the guidance and advice of the Assistant Deputy Registrar General when ambiguous situations render the interpretation and application of the guidelines difficult. In view of all the above, the government now considers this matter closed.
